I’m not convinced that the growth scare is warranted, or at least that it will be bad enough to change the direction of interest rates. If investors are worried about growth, why is breadth ample? Looking at the chart below, the tariff tantrum in the spring of last year was a proper growth scare and produced a 20% drawdown in the AI/ex-AI pair while breadth was very weak at 19%. Today we have a 22% drawdown and 61% breadth. Of course, the SPX is down only 3.4% today vs 21% last year April, but that distinction also tells me that this an AI-only scare and not a broader growth scare. 🧵(2/2)

The AI/ex-AI pair has now corrected 22% from its recent high, while simultaneously the 10-year Treasury yield is down 43 bps from its recent high of 5.36%. Coincidence? Probably not. BREAKING: US federal debt surged +$422 billion in October, to a record $40.6 trillion.

Since July 1st alone, US federal debt has soared +$1.2 trillion, averaging +$300 billion per month.

This is equivalent to an increase of ~$10 billion per day.

As a result, the US total public Debt-to-GDP ratio is up to 123%, the highest since the 2020 pandemic peak.

Meanwhile, the Treasury borrowed a record $839 billion through auctions of Treasury bills and notes last week, with the majority going toward repaying holders of maturing bills.

This surpassed the previous all-time high of $834 billion set during the same period in 2025.

The US debt crisis is in full-swing.

It's officially election day.

History says stocks are heading higher.

In fact, the S&P 500 has closed GREEN in the year following every US Midterm election since 1980.

As we noted in our analysis yesterday, we believe recent weakness in markets is largely a function of the uncertainty around Midterm elections.

However, when this uncertainty dissipates, markets react positively.

Since 1980, the S&P 500 has averaged a +14% gain in the 12 months following US Midterm elections.

Furthermore, even after divided-government outcomes, the index has averaged a +15% one-year gain, compared to +12% under single-party control.

Of course, the near-term picture will come with volatility and change.

But, if history is any guide, it's a great time to be bullish.
